correctness.rationale: For a symmetric normalized radius-one kernel, write endpoint weight \(a\) and \(b=4a\). Plancherel reduces the norm exactly to \(2^k\max_{0\le t\le1}t^r|1-bt|\). When \(b\le1\), pointwise monotonicity in \(b\) forces the best value at \(b=1\), and differentiation gives the unique interior maximum \(c_r\); Fourier nonnegativity is exactly \(b\le1\). When \(b>1\), the positive branch has maximum \(c_rb^{-r}\) at \(t=r/((r+1)b)\), while the negative branch is increasing and has maximum \(b-1\) at \(t=1\). Their unique crossing gives the unique global minimizer and the displayed equation. Setting \(y=r(b_r-1)\) gives \(y(1+y/r)^r=rc_r\to e^{-1}\), hence \(y\to W(e^{-1})\) and the two asymptotics follow. The packaged numerical verifier is consistent with these exact branch formulas but is not needed for the proof.
correctness.risk: The proof depends crucially on support radius one, where the normalized symmetric kernel has a single free scalar.

value.rationale: Support radius one is the first nontrivial averaging window and gives a natural boundary of the general smoothest-average problem. Solving it for every derivative order provides exact sharp constants and optimizers in rows where arbitrary-radius questions remain substantially harder, and the Lambert-\(W\) limit gives a clean quantitative comparison between unrestricted and Fourier-positive smoothing. This is a natural complete classification, not an arbitrary slice.
value.risk: The one-dimensional minimax reduction makes the proof elementary compared with the general-radius problem.

final_claim: For every integer \(k\ge1\), among symmetric normalized kernels supported on \(\{-1,0,1\}\), writing \(r=k/2\) and \(c_r=r^r/(r+1)^{r+1}\), the unrestricted sharp minimizer has endpoint parameter \(b_r>1\) determined uniquely by \((b_r-1)b_r^r=c_r\) and sharp constant \(2^k(b_r-1)\). Under \(\widehat u\ge0\), the unique minimizer for every \(k\) is the triangle kernel \((1/4,1/2,1/4)\) with sharp constant \(2^kc_r\). The asymptotic ratio tends to \(eW(e^{-1})\).
limitations: No claim is made for support radius greater than one.
Low-order instances covered by prior broader-radius theorems are treated as prior consistency cases, not as novelty.
